title: Rolling windows
summary: Moving averages, expanding windows and spotting unusual days.

steps.title: Smoothing with a moving average
body: Daily numbers are noisy: weekends dip, one big order makes a spike. A **rolling window** looks at the last *n* rows
for every row and aggregates them:
s.rolling(7).mean()      # average of this day and the 6 before it
The first 6 results are NaN, because there aren't 7 values yet. A 7-day window over daily data also cancels the
weekday pattern, since every window holds exactly one of each weekday. That's why dashboards show "7-day average".

steps.explain: Each result uses the current row and the ones before it. Until a full window exists the result is NaN.

steps.prompt: Daily sales are high on Saturdays and low on Mondays. Which smoothing makes the underlying trend easiest to see?
steps.explain: A window of 7 contains each weekday exactly once, so the weekly cycle averages out. 3 or 10 days contain an uneven mix of weekdays.

steps.title: Window options and expanding
body: s.rolling(7, min_periods=1).mean()   # no leading NaN: use what's there
s.rolling(7, center=True).mean()     # window centred on the row (for charts, not forecasts)
s.expanding().max()                  # everything so far: the record to date
Watch out when you use a window to **judge** today: `s.rolling(7).mean()` includes today itself. To compare today
with the days *before* it, shift first: `s.shift(1).rolling(7).mean()`.

steps.prompt: Match each expression to what it gives for every row.
pairs: mean of this row and the 6 before, NaN until 7 exist
mean of up to the last 7 rows, no leading NaN
mean of the 7 rows before this one

steps.title: Smooth it
prompt: Write `smooth(s, window)` that returns the rolling mean of `s` over `window` rows, **without** leading NaN
(use as many values as exist at the start), rounded to 2 decimals.

steps.explain: `cumsum` keeps adding; `expanding().max()` is the record so far (returned as floats).

steps.prompt: Flag a day as a spike when it is more than 3 standard deviations from the mean of the 7 days **before** it.
steps.explain: Shifting first keeps today's value out of its own yardstick: a huge spike would otherwise inflate the mean and std it is compared with.

steps.title: New records
prompt: Write `record_days(s)`. `s` is a Series of daily values with a DatetimeIndex. Return the list of dates (as `"YYYY-MM-DD"`
strings) on which the value was **strictly higher than every earlier day**. The first day always counts.
hints: The best value *before* each day is `s.cummax().shift(1)` (or `s.expanding().max().shift(1)`).
The first day has NaN there, so include it with `.isna() | (s > best_before)`.
Select dates with `s.index[mask]` and format with `.strftime("%Y-%m-%d")`.
template: Dojo.eq("the example (a tie is not a record)", ["2024-03-01", "2024-03-03", "2024-03-05"], record_days(dojo_s))

steps.title: Spot the unusual days
prompt: Write `flag_spikes(s, window=7, k=3)`. For each day, take the mean and standard deviation of the `window` days **before**
it (not including the day itself). Return the dates (as `"YYYY-MM-DD"` strings) whose value is more than `k` standard
deviations away from that mean, in either direction. Days without a full window before them are never flagged.
The tests use 40 days of noisy readings around 100 with one surge and one drop hidden in them.
hints: `past = s.shift(1).rolling(window)` gives windows of the days before.
`mask = (s - past.mean()).abs() > k * past.std()`; NaN comparisons are False, so short windows are never flagged.
template: Dojo.eq("finds the surge and the drop", ['2024-04-21', '2024-05-01', '2024-05-04'], flag_spikes(dojo_s))
Dojo.eq("nothing in a flat-ish series", [], flag_spikes(pd.Series([10.0, 11, 10, 11, 10, 11, 10, 11, 10, 11]), window=4))
Dojo.eq("a smaller window", ["2024-01-05"], flag_spikes(pd.Series([10.0, 11, 10, 11, 30, 11], index=pd.date_range("2024-01-01", periods=6, freq="D")), window=3))
